Pediatric Neurosurgery Artificial Intelligence Review Reveals High Accuracy but Validation Shortfalls

A comprehensive systematic review synthesizing research on computational decision support across pediatric neurosurgery has demonstrated that artificial intelligence models achieve notable precision in anatomical image segmentation and diagnostic tumor classification, while simultaneously identifying pervasive methodological limitations that currently restrict their readiness for routine operative deployment. Published in the Egyptian Journal of Neurosurgery by researchers Ravi Yadav, Debasrita Banerjee, and Jatin Kataria, the investigation gathered and analyzed published clinical investigations tracking pediatric patients eighteen years of age or younger who underwent diagnostic or surgical management for major intracranial conditions. By compiling and assessing twenty eligible investigations encompassing diagnostic imaging, procedural planning, and prognostic risk modeling, the systematic analysis determined that modern deep learning neural networks frequently matched expert radiological benchmarks when delineating fluid compartments or categorizing malignant neoplasms. However, the synthesis established that the prevailing scientific literature remains overwhelmingly dominated by retrospective, single-institution cohorts that seldom incorporate independent external cohort validation or formal probability calibration, indicating that while algorithmic tools exhibit substantial investigative promise, they should presently function strictly as supplementary decision-support aids rather than autonomous clinical mechanisms.

To rigorously evaluate the current scope and efficacy of artificial intelligence and machine learning architectures within this specialized surgical field, the investigative team executed an exhaustive literature search across five major international electronic repositories, including MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore. The investigative timeframe spanned from the inception of each respective electronic database up to August 31, 2025, capturing all human clinical reports conducted in English-language publications that addressed individuals aged eighteen years or younger. Initial computerized screening operations retrieved 1,345 candidate citations, which were reduced to 900 unique entries following the systematic elimination of 445 duplicate records. Dual independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts against predefined criteria using standardized forms, removing 812 records that failed to satisfy inclusion standards, before subjecting 88 full-length manuscripts to granular methodological scrutiny. In total, 20 clinical studies met all inclusion requirements under the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, comprising 8 investigations dedicated to pediatric hydrocephalus, 6 addressing pediatric brain neoplasms, 2 examining epilepsy surgical management, and 4 centered on traumatic brain injuries or neonatal hemorrhagic damage.

Within the diagnostic neuroimaging domain, computational convolutional neural networks and advanced deep learning pipelines displayed exceptional diagnostic fidelity when delineating fluid-filled intracranial compartments in pediatric hydrocephalus. Specific studies examined in the review highlighted automated segmentation architectures capable of tracking ventricular cerebrospinal fluid with remarkable volumetric precision, such as the U-Net convolutional neural network evaluated by Klimont and colleagues that achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient approximating 0.95 on an independent test set. Parallel efforts by Grimm and collaborators utilized transfer learning mechanisms incorporating labels derived from hidden Markov random field algorithms to segment brain and cerebrospinal fluid volumes on magnetic resonance imaging scans in 43 pediatric hydrocephalus patients. Expanding upon these structural models, Quon and colleagues demonstrated that deep learning volumetry exceeded traditional segmentation algorithms in accuracy and computational speed for obstructive hydrocephalus, providing clinically practical data to assist surgical interventions. Furthermore, an evaluation by Sekkat and colleagues applying a VGG16 convolutional architecture across 13,600 pediatric head computed tomography images yielded overall detection accuracies between 90 and 95 percent, alongside receiver operating characteristic curves approaching 1.0, substantiating the reliability of deep learning for automated ventricular volumetry.

In pediatric neuro-oncology, artificial intelligence tools extended beyond morphological segmentation to address non-invasive tumor typing, biological subgroup identification, and radiological prognosis using multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging and diffusion-weighted data. Research conducted by Novak and colleagues across 124 pediatric patients demonstrated that naive Bayes and random forest classifiers utilizing apparent diffusion coefficient histogram metrics achieved diagnostic classification accuracies between 84 and 85 percent when discriminating posterior fossa neoplasms. In a radiogenomics study led by Zhang and colleagues encompassing 263 pediatric patients, pre-operative magnetic resonance imaging scans analyzed by sequential machine learning classifiers achieved a micro-averaged F1 score of 88 percent in identifying medulloblastoma molecular subgroups, attaining particularly robust discriminatory capacity for Wingless-related integration site tumors. Semantic segmentation pipelines presented by Cariola and associates using data from the BraTS-PEDs 2024 challenge verified the feasibility of delineating complex tumor subregions, including whole tumor, enhancing margins, and core components. Complementing these diagnostic classifiers, vision transformer architectures tested by Tampu and colleagues incorporating patient age fusion demonstrated enhanced classification across diverse pediatric brain tumors, while radiomics-based nomograms developed by Luo and Lu showed that integrating clinical markers with imaging signatures improved two-year recurrence and survival stratification in medulloblastoma.

In the domain of surgical candidate selection and operative workflow optimization, investigators observed that algorithmic natural language processing algorithms can systematically detect surgical candidates who might otherwise experience prolonged evaluation delays. Cohen and colleagues demonstrated that applying machine learning classifiers to unstructured electronic health record clinical narratives yielded F-measures ranging from 0.71 to 0.82 when identifying pediatric patients eligible for epilepsy surgery, effectively identifying appropriate surgical candidates prior to their documented referral dates and outperforming baseline inter-annotator concordance. Building upon narrative extraction models, a multicenter randomized controlled trial conducted by Wissel and colleagues examined an automated clinical decision support system directly integrated within institutional electronic health records. Screening 4,858 pediatric patients with epilepsy, the trial randomized 284 identified surgical candidates in a two-to-one ratio between automated electronic provider alerts and standard clinical care. Pediatric patients assigned to algorithmic alerts achieved a statistically significant tripling in presurgical neurosurgical referral rates, documenting 9.8 percent in the intervention arm compared to 3.1 percent in standard care, accompanied by an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.21 that culminated in a greater number of completed surgical resections.
